title: IL SB1920: SCH CD-ASL IMPLEMENTATION

obligations: State Board of Education shall develop statewide guidance for school districts and educators on the use of artificial intelligence in elementary and secondary education, in consultation with stakeholders (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)).
The guidance shall include explanations of basic artificial intelligence concepts, including machine learning, natural language processing, and computer vision (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)(1)).

The guidance shall include specific ways artificial intelligence can be used at the district, school, and classroom levels to inform teaching and learning practices while preserving the human relationships essential to effective teaching and learning (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)(2)).

The guidance shall include how districts and educators can evaluate and address bias, privacy, transparency, and risk assessment and management in the usage of artificial intelligence technologies and applications (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)(3)).

The guidance shall include the impact of artificial intelligence on student data privacy, including federal and State statutes associated with student data privacy that are important to be aware of when setting policy for the use of artificial intelligence technologies in schools, such as the federal Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act of 1974, the federal Children's Internet Protection Act, the federal Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998, the Illinois School Student Records Act, and the Student Online Personal Protection Act (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)(4)).

The guidance shall include best practices for developing student literacy in artificial intelligence and engaging students in age appropriate discussions on the responsible and ethical use of artificial intelligence (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)(5)).

The guidance shall include best practices for making age appropriate and developmentally appropriate artificial intelligence applications available and accessible to all students (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)(6)).
The guidance shall include best practices and effective strategies for supporting special populations, such as English learners and students with disabilities (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)(7)).

The guidance shall include the impacts that the use of artificial intelligence may have in an educational setting, such as unintentional and disparate biases against special populations inherent within artificial intelligence products (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)(8)).

The guidance shall include resources and support available for districts, including the State Board of Education's Learning Technology Center, for the implementation of artificial intelligence in educational settings (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)(9)).
State Board of Education shall develop and publish this guidance by July 1, 2026 and provide continuous updates as it deems necessary (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)).

State Superintendent of Education may convene stakeholders for a statewide council to consult on the further development of guidance, resources, and other support for school districts and educators on the use of artificial intelligence in schools (Sec. 2-3.118a(b)).
The council must include individuals with expertise in artificial intelligence and no fewer than 2 currently practicing classroom teachers (Sec. 2-3.118a(b)).

The council shall represent the ethnic, racial, and geographic diversity of this State and include expertise across early childhood and elementary, middle, and high school settings (Sec. 2-3.118a(b)).
State Board of Education shall encourage school districts to collect teaching resources to support American Sign Language programs no later than July 1, 2026 (Sec. 2-3.206).

The teaching resources may include the importance and benefits of American Sign Language instruction for early ages and the prevalence of American Sign Language in the United States (Sec. 2-3.206(1)).
The teaching resources may include information on ways to implement American Sign Language instruction into the kindergarten through grade 8 curriculum (Sec. 2-3.206(2)).
The teaching resources may include information on how to properly administer American Sign Language instruction for students in kindergarten through grade 8 (Sec. 2-3.206(3)).

State Board of Education, in consultation with the State Educator Preparation and Licensure Board, shall design and implement a system of examinations, which shall be required prior to the issuance of educator licenses (Sec. 21B-30(b)).
State Board of Education may adopt such rules as may be necessary to implement and administer this Section (Sec. 21B-30(b)).
State Board must adopt rules to implement a paraprofessional competency test (Sec. 21B-30(c-5)).
All applicants seeking a State license shall be required to pass a test of content area knowledge for each area of endorsement for which there is an applicable test (Sec. 21B-30(d)).

State Board shall consult with any applicable vendors within 90 days after July 28, 2023 to develop a plan to transition the test of content area knowledge in the endorsement area of elementary education, grades one through 6, by July 1, 2026 to a content area test that contains testing elements that cover bilingualism, biliteracy, oral language development, foundational literacy skills, and developmentally appropriate higher order comprehension and on which a valid and reliable language and literacy subscore can be determined (Sec. 21B-30(d-5)).

State Board shall base its rules concerning the passing subscore on the language and literacy portion of the test on the recommended cut score determined in the formal standard setting process (Sec. 21B-30(d-5)).
State Board shall aggregate and publish the number of candidates in each preparation program who take the test and the number who pass the language and literacy portion (Sec. 21B-30(d-5)).

Beginning on September 1, 2015 until August 4, 2023 and beginning again on September 1, 2025, all candidates completing teacher preparation programs in this State and all candidates subject to Section 21B-35 of this Code are required to pass a teacher performance assessment approved by the State Board of Education, in consultation with the State Educator Preparation and Licensure Board (Sec. 21B-30(f)).

Subject to appropriation, an individual who holds a Professional Educator License and is employed for a minimum of one school year by a school district designated as Tier 1 under Section 18-8.15 may, after application to the State Board, receive from the State Board a refund for any costs associated with completing the teacher performance assessment under this subsection (Sec. 21B-30(f)).

Teacher Performance Assessment Task Force is created to evaluate potential performance based and objective teacher performance assessment systems for implementation across all educator preparation programs in this State, with the intention of ensuring consistency across programs and supporting a thoughtful and well rounded licensure system (Sec. 21B-30(f-5)).
Members appointed to the Task Force must reflect the racial, ethnic, and geographic diversity of this State (Sec. 21B-30(f-5)).
Task Force shall consist of all of the members listed in items (1) through (25) of this subsection (Sec. 21B-30(f-5)).
Members of the Task Force shall serve without compensation (Sec. 21B-30(f-5)).

Task Force shall first meet at the call of the State Superintendent of Education, and each subsequent meeting shall be called by the chairperson of the Task Force, who shall be designated by the State Superintendent of Education (Sec. 21B-30(f-5)).
State Board of Education shall provide administrative and other support to the Task Force (Sec. 21B-30(f-5)).

On or before October 31, 2024, the Task Force shall report on its work, including recommendations on a teacher performance assessment system in this State, to the State Board of Education and the General Assembly (Sec. 21B-30(f-5)).
Task Force is dissolved upon submission of this report (Sec. 21B-30(f-5)).

Content area knowledge test and the teacher performance assessment shall be the tests that from time to time are designated by the State Board of Education, in consultation with the State Educator Preparation and Licensure Board, and may be tests prepared by an educational testing organization or tests designed by the State Board of Education, in consultation with the State Educator Preparation and Licensure Board (Sec. 21B-30(g)).
Test of content area knowledge shall assess content knowledge in a specific subject field (Sec. 21B-30(g)).

Tests must be designed to be racially neutral to ensure that no person taking the tests is discriminated against on the basis of race, color, national origin, or other factors unrelated to the person's ability to perform as a licensed employee (Sec. 21B-30(g)).
Score required to pass the tests shall be fixed by the State Board of Education, in consultation with the State Educator Preparation and Licensure Board (Sec. 21B-30(g)).
State Board of Education's rules for scoring the content area knowledge test may include scoring and retaking of each test section separately and independently (Sec. 21B-30(g)).

Tests shall be administered not fewer than 3 times a year at such time and place as may be designated by the State Board of Education, in consultation with the State Educator Preparation and Licensure Board (Sec. 21B-30(g)).

State Board shall implement a test or tests to assess the speaking, reading, writing, and grammar skills of applicants for an endorsement or a license issued under subdivision (G) of paragraph (2) of Section 21B-20 of this Code in the English language and in the language of the transitional bilingual education program requested by the applicant (Sec. 21B-30(g)).

On or before July 1, 2026, the State Board of Education shall post publicly on its website the process by which the State Board or any entity designated by the State Board evaluates content area knowledge tests to determine content validity, an absence of bias, or the scores required to pass such tests (Sec. 21B-30(g-5)).

State Board shall also make the following information publicly available on its website: the process by which members are selected to form a committee or group to make the determinations set forth in this subsection (g-5); and the agenda and summary of each meeting of any such committee or group (Sec. 21B-30(g-5)(1)-(2)).
Except as provided in Section 34-6 of this Code, the provisions of this Section shall apply equally in any school district subject to Article 34 of this Code (Sec. 21B-30(h)).

Rules developed to implement and enforce the testing requirements under this Section shall include, without limitation, provisions governing test selection, test validation, and determination of a passing score, administration of the tests, frequency of administration, applicant fees, frequency of applicants taking the tests, the years for which a score is valid, and appropriate special accommodations (Sec. 21B-30(i)).
State Board of Education shall develop such rules as may be needed to ensure uniformity from year to year in the level of difficulty for each form of an assessment (Sec. 21B-30(i)).
Each school may adopt an age appropriate curriculum for Internet safety instruction of students in grades kindergarten through 12 (Sec. 27-13.3(c)).

Beginning with the 2009-2010 school year, a school district must incorporate into the school curriculum a component on Internet safety to be taught at least once each school year to students in grades 3 through 12 (Sec. 27-13.3(c)).
School board shall determine the scope and duration of this unit of instruction (Sec. 27-13.3(c)).

The age appropriate unit of instruction may be incorporated into the current courses of study regularly taught in the district's schools, as determined by the school board, and it is recommended that the unit of instruction include the topics listed in items (1) through (7) of this subsection (Sec. 27-13.3(c)).

The recommended topics include safe and responsible use of social networking websites, chat rooms, electronic mail, bulletin boards, instant messaging, and other means of communication on the Internet (Sec. 27-13.3(c)(1)).
The recommended topics include recognizing, avoiding, and reporting online solicitations of students, their classmates, and their friends by sexual predators (Sec. 27-13.3(c)(2)).
The recommended topics include risks of transmitting personal information on the Internet (Sec. 27-13.3(c)(3)).
The recommended topics include recognizing and avoiding unsolicited or deceptive communications received online (Sec. 27-13.3(c)(4)).

The recommended topics include recognizing and reporting online harassment and cyberbullying, including the creation and distribution of false representations of individuals created by artificial intelligence, including, but not limited to, sexually explicit images and videos (Sec. 27-13.3(c)(5)).
The recommended topics include reporting illegal activities and communications on the Internet (Sec. 27-13.3(c)(6)).
The recommended topics include copyright laws on written materials, photographs, music, and video (Sec. 27-13.3(c)(7)).
Curricula devised in accordance with subsection (c) of this Section may be submitted for review to the Office of the Illinois Attorney General (Sec. 27-13.3(d)).

State Board of Education shall make available resource materials for educating children regarding child online safety and may take into consideration the curriculum on this subject developed by other states, as well as any other curricular materials suggested by education experts, child psychologists, or technology companies that work on child online safety issues (Sec. 27-13.3(e)).

Materials may include without limitation safe online communications, privacy protection, cyberbullying, viewing inappropriate material, file sharing, and the importance of open communication with responsible adults (Sec. 27-13.3(e)).
State Board of Education shall make these resource materials available on its Internet website (Sec. 27-13.3(e)).
prohibitions: There shall be no exception to the requirement that all applicants seeking a State license pass a test of content area knowledge for each area of endorsement for which there is an applicable test (Sec. 21B-30(d)).
A candidate may not be required to submit test materials by video submission (Sec. 21B-30(f)).

Beginning on August 4, 2023 through August 31, 2025, no candidate completing a teacher preparation program in this State or candidate subject to Section 21B-35 of this Code is required to pass a teacher performance assessment (Sec. 21B-30(f)).
Candidates need not achieve a particular subscore in the area of language and literacy (Sec. 21B-30(d-5)).

Tests must be designed to be racially neutral to ensure that no person taking the tests is discriminated against on the basis of race, color, national origin, or other factors unrelated to the person's ability to perform as a licensed employee (Sec. 21B-30(g)).

compliance_steps: Monitor the State Board of Education website for the statewide AI guidance, which must be published by July 1, 2026 (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)).

Review the guidance once published, including the required topics on AI concepts, specific uses, bias, privacy, transparency, risk assessment, student data privacy laws, best practices for student literacy, accessibility, special populations, and resources (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)(1)-(9)).

Evaluate any AI tools or applications used in the district against the guidance, particularly regarding bias, privacy, transparency, risk management, and compliance with federal and State student data privacy statutes such as FERPA, CIPA, COPPA, the Illinois School Student Records Act, and the Student Online Personal Protection Act (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)(3)-(4)).

Ensure that any AI deployment does not produce unintentional disparate biases against special populations such as English learners and students with disabilities, as the guidance will address these impacts (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)(7)-(8)).

Incorporate into the school curriculum a component on Internet safety at least once each school year for grades 3 through 12, including recognizing and reporting online harassment and cyberbullying, and specifically the creation and distribution of false representations of individuals created by artificial intelligence, including sexually explicit images and videos (Sec. 27-13.3(c), Sec. 27-13.3(c)(5)).

If the organisation is involved in educator preparation or testing, comply with the testing requirements in Section 21B-30, including content area knowledge tests, teacher performance assessment timelines, racial neutrality, and public posting of test evaluation processes by July 1, 2026 (Sec. 21B-30(d), (f), (g), (g-5)).
For school districts, collect teaching resources to support American Sign Language programs as encouraged by the State Board no later than July 1, 2026 (Sec. 2-3.206).

reading.penalties_and_enforcement: The statute does not specify penalties, enforcement authority, or a private right of action. The State Board of Education is directed to adopt rules to implement and administer the testing requirements under Section 21B-30 (Sec. 21B-30(b), Sec. 21B-30(i)). The State Board is also directed to develop and publish AI guidance (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)). No enforcement mechanism for the AI guidance or ASL resource encouragement is stated.
how_it_affects_ai_deployment: School districts and educators will receive statewide guidance on the use of artificial intelligence in elementary and secondary education, which must include explanations of AI concepts, specific ways to use AI, evaluation of bias, privacy, transparency, risk assessment and management, impact on student data privacy, best practices for student literacy, accessibility, special populations, and available resources (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)).

The guidance must address federal and State student data privacy statutes such as the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, the Children's Internet Protection Act, the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, the Illinois School Student Records Act, and the Student Online Personal Protection Act, so any AI deployment in schools must be evaluated against these laws (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)(4)).

The guidance will include how districts and educators can evaluate and address bias, privacy, transparency, and risk assessment and management in AI usage, meaning AI tools used in schools may be subject to scrutiny for these issues (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)(3)).

The guidance will include impacts of AI on special populations and unintentional disparate biases, so AI products used in schools may need to address bias against English learners and students with disabilities (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)(7)-(8)).

School districts must incorporate into their curriculum a component on Internet safety that includes recognizing and reporting online harassment and cyberbullying, including the creation and distribution of false representations of individuals created by artificial intelligence, including sexually explicit images and videos (Sec. 27-13.3(c)(5)). This means AI generated deepfakes or false images are explicitly part of required internet safety education, and organisations deploying AI that could create such content may be implicated in school policies.

The State Board may convene a statewide council with AI expertise and classroom teachers to further develop guidance, resources, and support for AI use in schools, which could influence expectations for AI deployment (Sec. 2-3.118a(b)).

The law does not impose direct requirements on private AI developers or vendors; it directs the State Board to create guidance and requires school districts to teach about AI related risks (Sec. 2-3.118a(a), Sec. 27-13.3(c)).

What it does

This Illinois law directs the State Board of Education to develop and publish statewide guidance for school districts and educators on the use of artificial intelligence in elementary and secondary education by July 1, 2026. It also requires the State Board to encourage school districts to collect teaching resources for American Sign Language programs, amends educator testing requirements, and updates internet safety curriculum to include artificial intelligence generated false representations. The law does not impose direct requirements on private AI developers but shapes how schools evaluate and teach about AI.

Who it applies to

  • State Board of Education
  • school districts
  • educators
  • candidates for educator licenses
  • teacher preparation programs
  • State Educator Preparation and Licensure Board
  • State Superintendent of Education
  • school boards
  • students in grades 3 through 12 for internet safety curriculum

  • Beginning on August 4, 2023 through August 31, 2025, no candidate completing a teacher preparation program in this State or candidate subject to Section 21B-35 of this Code is required to pass a teacher performance assessment (Sec. 21B-30(f)).
  • Candidates need not achieve a particular subscore in the area of language and literacy (Sec. 21B-30(d-5)).
  • Tests must be designed to be racially neutral to ensure that no person taking the tests is discriminated against on the basis of race, color, national origin, or other factors unrelated to the person's ability to perform as a licensed employee (Sec. 21B-30(g)).

Penalties and enforcement

The statute does not specify penalties, enforcement authority, or a private right of action. The State Board of Education is directed to adopt rules to implement and administer the testing requirements under Section 21B-30 (Sec. 21B-30(b), Sec. 21B-30(i)). The State Board is also directed to develop and publish AI guidance (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)). No enforcement mechanism for the AI guidance or ASL resource encouragement is stated.

How it affects AI deployment

  • School districts and educators will receive statewide guidance on the use of artificial intelligence in elementary and secondary education, which must include explanations of AI concepts, specific ways to use AI, evaluation of bias, privacy, transparency, risk assessment and management, impact on student data privacy, best practices for student literacy, accessibility, special populations, and available resources (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)).
  • The guidance must address federal and State student data privacy statutes such as the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, the Children's Internet Protection Act, the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, the Illinois School Student Records Act, and the Student Online Personal Protection Act, so any AI deployment in schools must be evaluated against these laws (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)(4)).
  • The guidance will include how districts and educators can evaluate and address bias, privacy, transparency, and risk assessment and management in AI usage, meaning AI tools used in schools may be subject to scrutiny for these issues (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)(3)).
  • The guidance will include impacts of AI on special populations and unintentional disparate biases, so AI products used in schools may need to address bias against English learners and students with disabilities (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)(7)-(8)).
  • School districts must incorporate into their curriculum a component on Internet safety that includes recognizing and reporting online harassment and cyberbullying, including the creation and distribution of false representations of individuals created by artificial intelligence, including sexually explicit images and videos (Sec. 27-13.3(c)(5)). This means AI generated deepfakes or false images are explicitly part of required internet safety education, and organisations deploying AI that could create such content may be implicated in school policies.
  • The State Board may convene a statewide council with AI expertise and classroom teachers to further develop guidance, resources, and support for AI use in schools, which could influence expectations for AI deployment (Sec. 2-3.118a(b)).
  • The law does not impose direct requirements on private AI developers or vendors; it directs the State Board to create guidance and requires school districts to teach about AI related risks (Sec. 2-3.118a(a), Sec. 27-13.3(c)).

Notable exemptions

  • Candidates need not achieve a particular subscore in the area of language and literacy (Sec. 21B-30(d-5)).
  • Beginning on August 4, 2023 through August 31, 2025, no candidate completing a teacher preparation program in this State or candidate subject to Section 21B-35 of this Code is required to pass a teacher performance assessment (Sec. 21B-30(f)).
  • Except as provided in Section 34-6 of this Code, the provisions of this Section shall apply equally in any school district subject to Article 34 of this Code (Sec. 21B-30(h)).

Compliance steps

  • Monitor the State Board of Education website for the statewide AI guidance, which must be published by July 1, 2026 (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)).
  • Review the guidance once published, including the required topics on AI concepts, specific uses, bias, privacy, transparency, risk assessment, student data privacy laws, best practices for student literacy, accessibility, special populations, and resources (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)(1)-(9)).
  • Evaluate any AI tools or applications used in the district against the guidance, particularly regarding bias, privacy, transparency, risk management, and compliance with federal and State student data privacy statutes such as FERPA, CIPA, COPPA, the Illinois School Student Records Act, and the Student Online Personal Protection Act (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)(3)-(4)).
  • Ensure that any AI deployment does not produce unintentional disparate biases against special populations such as English learners and students with disabilities, as the guidance will address these impacts (Sec. 2-3.118a(a)(7)-(8)).
  • Incorporate into the school curriculum a component on Internet safety at least once each school year for grades 3 through 12, including recognizing and reporting online harassment and cyberbullying, and specifically the creation and distribution of false representations of individuals created by artificial intelligence, including sexually explicit images and videos (Sec. 27-13.3(c), Sec. 27-13.3(c)(5)).
  • If the organisation is involved in educator preparation or testing, comply with the testing requirements in Section 21B-30, including content area knowledge tests, teacher performance assessment timelines, racial neutrality, and public posting of test evaluation processes by July 1, 2026 (Sec. 21B-30(d), (f), (g), (g-5)).
  • For school districts, collect teaching resources to support American Sign Language programs as encouraged by the State Board no later than July 1, 2026 (Sec. 2-3.206).
